summary:
**Mission Architect** is a browser-based game, playable on phone or desktop, that lets a student design, launch and fly a complete space mission. The player picks a target (Lunar Lander, Mars Orbiter or Europa Explorer) and a difficulty. They then build the spacecraft from six subsystem choices: launch vehicle, propulsion, power, communications, payload and safety. A go/no-go poll gives a survival estimate before launch. The flight runs ten events and three live calls, and a debrief scores the result and ranks the player.

Real missions balance mass, power, communications, instruments, launch vehicle and budget all at once, yet classrooms teach each idea alone, so the links between them stay abstract. In the game, changing one choice visibly moves the others, so players see the coupling directly.

It is also grounded in real physics. The game's ∆V matches the rocket equation: 2,302 m/s by hand and in the game. Solar power follows the inverse-square law, as on Juno and Europa Clipper. Across 19,800 simulated flights there were no errors, and the best build at each target succeeded 89–94% of the time.

It matters because it turns systems engineering into something students can try and learn from, not just read about.
details: Mission Architect is a game that runs in any browser on phone or desktop, with no installation. A player goes through five steps: Choose a target (Lunar Lander, Mars Orbiter or Europa Explorer) and a difficulty. Design the spacecraft from six decisions: launch vehicle, propulsion, power, communications, payload and safety. Live gauges track mass, cost, power and ∆V, and launch stays locked until every limit is met. Hold a go/no-go review, where five stations report GO, CAUTION or RISK and give a survival estimate. Fly ten events with three live calls. Get a debrief with a score, a rank and engineer’s notes. Benefits Students see how mass, power, communications, instruments, launch vehicle and budget affect each other, instead of meeting each idea alone as a formula. The numbers follow real physics. The ∆V matches the rocket equation (2,302 m/s by hand and in the game). Solar power follows the inverse-square law, as on Juno and Europa Clipper. Data return falls with distance. It was tested at scale: 19,800 simulated flights with no errors. Design quality decides the outcome. A minimal build succeeded 0% of the time, and the best build at each target succeeded 89–94%. Intended impact The aim is to make systems engineering something students can try and learn from. Planned next steps are a classroom mode with a shared seed and a class leaderboard, a teacher view of each team’s margins and loss causes, more targets such as asteroid sample return and Venus, and higher stakes for the in-flight calls. Tools, languages, hardware, software The deck only shows that the game runs in a browser and was tested with simulated flights and a scripted phone-size playthrough. Add your actual stack here, for example the front-end language, simulation scripts and test tools: [your stack]. Creativity It turns the coupling between constraints into a game loop, from design through to a debrief. Three destinations stretch the same rules in different directions. Each flight event has its own scene and a danger level. The score is built from science, budget, health and margins, with a rank ladder from Engineer to Flight Director. It checks itself against real missions such as Juno and Europa Clipper. Factors considered Playability: comms fall with distance to the power 1.5 instead of 2, so outer-planet missions stay winnable for beginners. Balance: testing found that auto-tuned fuel gave an 8% ∆V margin, below the 10% thin-margin rule. Raising the default margin to 15% cut mission losses by 74–81%. Europa’s science target was lowered from 80 to 50 after the best build topped out near 58. Known simplifications: bus mass and cost are fixed for every design, and event odds are tuned for play, not drawn from flight statistics. Mobile use: the game was tested on a phone-size screen.
